## Warm-up retrieval

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q1. A small *p*-value (e.g., $p = 0.001$) means:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The null hypothesis is true with probability 0.001</li>
  <li>The data would be unusual if the null hypothesis were true</li>
  <li>The alternative hypothesis is proven</li>
  <li>The chance the next study will replicate this result is high</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> $p$-values measure how surprising the data is *under* $H_0$, not the probability that $H_0$ is true. A small $p$-value is evidence against $H_0$, but it doesn't *prove* $H_a$ and doesn't tell you anything about the magnitude of the effect.</div>
:::


## What you'll be able to do

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Apply confidence intervals and hypothesis tests to regression coefficients (slope, intercept)
- Check the **LINE conditions** (Linearity, Independence, Normality, Equality of variance) for regression inference
- Compare *theory-based* and *simulation-based* approaches to regression inference
- Use diagnostic plots (residual vs. fitted, QQ-plot) to assess model assumptions

::: {.predict}
Before we begin: which of these objectives feels least familiar to you right now? Hold that in mind — we'll check back at the end.
:::

<div class="mcq-stem">Q3. A theory-based *t*-test and a simulation-based permutation test for a regression slope often yield similar p-values when:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The sample is very small</li>
  <li>The LINE conditions are met and the sample is reasonably large</li>
  <li>The model has many predictors</li>
  <li>The data is non-normal</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> When the assumptions hold and $n$ is reasonable, theory-based and simulation-based methods usually agree closely. They diverge most when assumptions fail — which is exactly when simulation-based methods earn their keep.</div>
:::

<div class="mcq-stem">Q4. A regression model has slope = 0.5 and p-value = 0.001. The MOST precise conclusion:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>The slope is exactly 0.5 in the population</li>
  <li>**There is strong evidence that the population slope is not zero — but our estimate of the slope (0.5) still carries uncertainty (use a CI to quantify it)**</li>
  <li>The slope is significant at any $\alpha$</li>
  <li>The relationship is causal</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> The point estimate is 0.5, but the population slope could plausibly be anywhere in the slope's CI. The p-value tests whether 0 is plausible, not whether 0.5 is correct.</div>
:::

:::


## Check-in: Theory-based inference for multiple linear regression

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="c"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q5. A residual plot shows residuals fanning OUT (small at low fitted values, large at high fitted values). This violates which LINE condition?</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Linearity</li>
  <li>Independence</li>
  <li>**Equal variance** — the &quot;E&quot; in LINE</li>
  <li>Normality</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(c)</strong> Funnel-shaped residual spread = unequal variance. The &quot;equal variance&quot; assumption requires residuals to have roughly the SAME spread across the range of fitted values. When that fails, the SEs reported by `lm()` (which assume equal variance) are unreliable, and the resulting CIs/tests can be miscalibrated. The simulation-based workflow from §10.3 (bootstrap CIs, permutation tests via `infer`) doesn't lean on equal variance and is a good fallback.</div>
:::

:::

## Check-in: Simulation-based Inference for multiple linear regression

::: {.predict}
Take 30 seconds. Predict your answer **before** clicking. Then tap your choice.
:::

::: {.mcq data-correct="b"}
<div class="mcq-stem">Q6. A QQ-plot of residuals shows points sharply deviating from the diagonal at both tails. This suggests:</div>
<ol class="mcq-options">
  <li>Linearity is violated</li>
  <li>**The residuals are not Normal — at the extremes, observed residuals are more extreme than a Normal distribution would predict**</li>
  <li>Equal variance is violated</li>
  <li>Independence is violated</li>
</ol>
<div class="mcq-controls">
<button class="poll-btn show-poll">Show class poll</button>
<button class="show-answer">Show answer</button>
</div>
<div class="poll-bar"></div>
<div class="mcq-reveal"><strong>(b)</strong> A QQ-plot lines up *observed quantiles* against *Normal quantiles*. When the tails of the cloud diverge from the diagonal, the actual residuals are more spread out at the extremes than a Normal distribution would predict — the &quot;N&quot; assumption is wobbly. Mild deviations are usually fine; extreme ones can make `lm()`'s theory-based CIs and $p$-values too aggressive (too narrow, too small) and the simulation-based workflow becomes the more honest choice.</div>
:::
